title: What Your First VC Meeting Has to Prove
summary: What Your First VC Meeting Has to Prove
body_markdown:
The best way to improve a pitch is to ask what the investor would have to believe to invest. Ask it before opening the deck. The answer will usually be two or three claims about the business. Most of the slides people spend the longest on don't test any of them.


Start with a short sentence about the customer and the change you make for them. “We help small freight brokers resolve disputed invoices before their customers' payment runs” is a better start than “we're modernizing logistics finance.” The first sentence gives an investor something to investigate. The second could belong to a dozen companies.


## Make the size of the bet clear


Read[how Khosla Ventures describes its investment decisions](https://www.khoslaventures.com/about/how-we-decide) before sending it a pitch. In particular, the firm distinguishes between seed investment for a science or business experiment and its other venture investments. That distinction is useful even if you never pitch Khosla. A pre-product science company and a software company with contracts both need evidence, but the evidence will be different.


Suppose your initial buyer is an independent freight broker. Show how many fit the first market and what buyers have actually paid or told you they'd pay. Then explain what would have to be true for you to expand. Which adjacent buyer faces the same problem? Does that buyer already get value from the same product, or would you have to build a new one? An honest narrow market and a plausible way out beats a giant top-down market with no path in.


## Bring evidence for the claim you're making


Pick each important claim and write the strongest evidence you have next to it. If you say the product saves a team seven hours, show who measured the time, which task they measured, and how many teams you've observed. If two teams use it every week but neither pays, say that. It tells an investor something useful: the product may be becoming a habit, but willingness to pay still needs a test.


Different companies should show different evidence. A technical breakthrough might be best explained by a reproducible test against a benchmark. A sales-led software company might show a renewal or a sale that happened without the founder’s personal connection. A consumer company might distinguish downloads from people who come back. The test is whether the evidence would convince a skeptical person who wasn't in the room when it happened.


[Vinod Khosla’s pitch masterclass](https://www.khoslaventures.com/posts/nail-your-raise-luring-vcs) is a useful second pass on the deck. Watch it after you have made your own list of claims. You’ll have a better idea which advice applies to the meeting you’re preparing for and which slides are taking up space.


## Say what the money buys


Imagine raising $2 million. The amount by itself doesn't tell anyone if the financing is a good bet. An operating plan might say it buys 15 months to take two unpaid pilots to paid rollouts, ship the missing integration, and learn whether a sales cycle under 90 days is repeatable. Those are example milestones, not benchmarks. The right ones would give the next investor a reason to change their mind.


Write down the fastest way the plan could fail. What if both pilots stall on security review? What if an apparent product problem turns out to be a procurement problem? Tie the risk to a decision: if neither customer has a sponsor and a date by month three, stop building the integration and revisit the buyer. The point is to spend the round learning the answer while you can still afford to change course.


## Make the meeting easy to repeat


Rehearse with someone who understands startups but has never heard of yours. Afterwards ask them to tell you what the company does, what you're raising, and what the money will prove. Listen without correcting them. Anything they miss is a good candidate to fix in the first two minutes of the pitch.


Keep a lightweight evidence worksheet alongside the deck: one row per claim, one link or document, one objection, and one concrete next test. In a meeting, the claims you've tested are the story. Afterward, the worksheet tells you what to learn next.
